rows: Identify loss of corneal transparency / subtle edema
Quantify endothelial cell density and morphology
Specular Reflection (Angle of Incidence = Angle of Reflection)

branches: Sclerotic Scatter: Light trapped in cornea via TIR until hit by opacity
Specular: Light reflects off the interface between aqueous (RI 1.336) and endothelium (RI 1.376)
Scattering: Occurs when collagen fibril spacing is disrupted (Edema/Scars)

sections.title: Sclerotic Scatter: Step-by-Step Technique
content: Step 1: Darken the exam room completely.
Step 2: Decouple the slit-lamp beam from the microscope.
Step 3: Direct a bright, narrow slit beam (2-3mm wide) onto the limbus.
Step 4: Ensure the light undergoes Total Internal Reflection through the cornea.
Step 5: Observe the cornea from the side (naked eye) or through the oculars at low magnification.
Step 6: Look for a 'Glow' or 'Halo' at the opposite limbus (indicating a clear cornea).

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Sclerotic Scatter: Reveals subtle microcystic edema often missed by direct focal illumination.
Sclerotic Scatter: Identifies 'Sattler’s Veil' (epithelial edema due to hypoxia or high IOP).
Specular Microscopy: Visualizes 'Guttata' (dark non-reflective spots on the mosaic).
Specular Microscopy: Detects 'Intracellular vacuoles' or 'Snail tracks' in trauma/inflammation.
Both: Crucial for pre-operative assessment of Fuchs' Endothelial Corneal Dystrophy (FECD).

sections.title: Red Flags: Endothelial Decompensation Signs
content: ECD < 500 cells/mm²: High risk for permanent corneal edema (Bullous Keratopathy).
CV > 0.40: Significant instability of the endothelial pump.
Pachymetry > 640 μm: High suspicion of clinical edema regardless of clarity.
Sclerotic Scatter: Visualization of 'striae' (Descemet's folds) indicates deep stromal edema.
Epithelial Bullae: End-stage endothelial failure.

sections.title: Surgical Decision Algorithm
content: 1. Perform Sclerotic Scatter: If haze is present, quantify with Specular Microscopy.
2. Assess ECD: If >1500, proceed with routine phacoemulsification.
3. Assess ECD: If 1000-1500, use 'soft-shell' viscoelastic technique and low ultrasound energy.
4. Assess ECD: If <800 OR CCT >620um, consider combined Phaco-DMEK/DSAEK (Triple Procedure).

content.explanation: P: Polymegethism (CV < 0.30); H: Hexagonality (> 60%); D: Density (> 2000 cells/mm²).

sections.title: Recent Advances: AI & Cell Imaging
content: Automated AI segmentation: Reduces manual marking errors in low-density counts.
Wide-field Specular Microscopy: Images larger areas to detect peripheral cell loss.
NICE Study Insights: Endothelial cell loss is highest in the first 3 months post-op.
Cell-Injection Therapy: Potential future replacement for DMEK/DSAEK.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Sclerotic scatter is the most sensitive 'quick' clinical screen for early Fuch's dystrophy.
If you see a 'black hole' on specular microscopy that isn't a guttata, consider a leukocyte or pigment clump.
Specular microscopy requires a clear cornea; if the cornea is too edematous, use Anterior Segment OCT (AS-OCT) instead.
Always adjust the patient's fixation to image the central, superior, and inferior endothelium separately.
A 'Hard' cataract requires more energy; if ECD is low, prioritize laser-assisted cataract surgery (FLACS) to protect the endothelium.

sections.title: Pediatric Considerations
sections.content: In children, ECD is significantly higher (often >3500 cells/mm²). Sclerotic scatter is vital in pediatric glaucoma cases to monitor for 'Haab Striae' or corneal enlargement (buphthalmos). Specular microscopy in children often requires hand-held units or sedation due to fixation requirements.
